claim: Fossil evidence of brood care behavior is exceptionally scarce.
source: However, fossil evidence of such a complex behavior is exceptionally scarce.
evidence: This is presented as established knowledge about the fossil record.

claim: Wathondara kotejai is an ensign scale insect from mid-Cretaceous Burmese amber.
source: Here, we report an ensign scale insect (Hemiptera: Ortheziidae), Wathondara kotejai gen. et sp. nov., from mid-Cretaceous Burmese amber, which preserves eggs within a wax ovisac, and several freshly hatched nymphs.
evidence: This is the primary finding of the study, supported by the fossil specimen described.

claim: Wathondara kotejai preserves eggs within a wax ovisac and several freshly hatched nymphs.
source: Here, we report an ensign scale insect (Hemiptera: Ortheziidae), Wathondara kotejai gen. et sp. nov., from mid-Cretaceous Burmese amber, which preserves eggs within a wax ovisac, and several freshly hatched nymphs.
evidence: This is directly observed in the fossil specimen.

claim: Wathondara kotejai is the only Mesozoic record of an adult female scale insect.
source: The new fossil is the only Mesozoic record of an adult female scale insect.
evidence: This is stated based on review of the fossil record.

claim: Wathondara kotejai represents the earliest unequivocal direct evidence of brood care in the insect fossil record.
source: More importantly, our finding represents the earliest unequivocal direct evidence of brood care in the insect fossil record and demonstrates a remarkably conserved egg-brooding reproductive strategy within scale insects in stasis for nearly 100 million years.
evidence: This is inferred from the age of the fossil and the presence of eggs and nymphs in the ovisac.

claim: The egg-brooding reproductive strategy within scale insects has been in stasis for nearly 100 million years.
source: More importantly, our finding represents the earliest unequivocal direct evidence of brood care in the insect fossil record and demonstrates a remarkably conserved egg-brooding reproductive strategy within scale insects in stasis for nearly 100 million years.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between the fossil behavior and modern scale insect behavior.

claim: Brood care is an altruistic trait that evolved to enhance the fitness of offspring at a cost to the parents.
source: Brood care is an altruistic trait that evolved to enhance the fitness of offspring at a cost to the parents and represents a breakthrough in the adaptation of organisms to their environment (Tallamy, 1984; Clutton-Brock, 1991; Gilbert and Manica, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fossil evidence of brood care has been reported mainly in dinosaurs, ostracods, and arachnids, but rarely in insects.
source: Fossil evidence of such an ephemeral behavior is extremely rare, reported mainly in dinosaurs (Meng et al., 2004; Varricchio et al., 2008), ostracods (Siveter et al., 2007, 2014), arachnids (Engel and Grimaldi, 2014), but rarely in insects.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fossil discoveries.

claim: Only two putative examples of brood care in Mesozoic insects have been described based on fossils until now.
source: Until now only two putative examples in Mesozoic insects have been described based on fossils (Peñalver et al., 2012; Cai et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Phylogenetic analyses suggest some ancient insects evolved brood care.
source: Although phylogenetic analyses suggest some ancient insects evolved brood care (e.g., Korb et al., 2012), only fossils provide unequivocal direct evidence.
evidence: This is supported by citation to phylogenetic analysis.

claim: Only fossils provide unequivocal direct evidence of brood care in ancient insects.
source: Although phylogenetic analyses suggest some ancient insects evolved brood care (e.g., Korb et al., 2012), only fossils provide unequivocal direct evidence.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle about the value of fossil evidence.

claim: Scale insects (Coccoidea) comprise about 7800 species.
source: Scale insects (Coccoidea), with about 7800 species, are highly diverse, and most of them are obligatory plant parasites often of economic importance (Ben-Dov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a reference work.

claim: Most scale insects are obligatory plant parasites often of economic importance.
source: Scale insects (Coccoidea), with about 7800 species, are highly diverse, and most of them are obligatory plant parasites often of economic importance (Ben-Dov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a reference work.

claim: Scale insects are considered some of the most evolutionarily fascinating organisms amongst insects.
source: They exhibit many unusual features of morphology, reproduction, and life history and are thus considered as some of the most evolutionarily fascinating organisms amongst insects (Wappler and Ben-Dov, 2008; Hodgson and Hardy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The female scale insect life cycle involves two or three actively feeding instars prior to the adult stage.
source: The female life cycle involves two or three actively feeding instars prior to the adult stage, and adult females are wingless, resembling the immature stages (Gullan and Cook, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Adult female scale insects are wingless and resemble the immature stages.
source: The female life cycle involves two or three actively feeding instars prior to the adult stage, and adult females are wingless, resembling the immature stages (Gullan and Cook, 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Adult male scale insects are delicate, ephemeral insects with simplified wing venation.
source: In contrast, adult males are delicate, ephemeral insects with simplified wing venation (Hodgson and Hardy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Scale insects separated from their sister-group, the aphids, at least by the Middle Permian.
source: Scale insects separated from their sister-group, the aphids, at least by the Middle Permian based on the earliest occurrence of Aphidomorpha (Szwedo et al., 2015), with the fossil record probably extending back to the Middle Triassic (trace fossils in Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to trace fossils.

claim: The scale insect fossil record probably extends back to the Middle Triassic.
source: Scale insects separated from their sister-group, the aphids, at least by the Middle Permian based on the earliest occurrence of Aphidomorpha (Szwedo et al., 2015), with the fossil record probably extending back to the Middle Triassic (trace fossils in Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by reference to trace fossils shown in Figure 4.

claim: The scale insect fossil record is over-dominated by males entrapped in fossil resins.
source: However, their fossil record is over-dominated by males entrapped in fossil resins, and fossil adult females are very scarce—probably because they are commonly sedentary or sessile on host plants (Koteja, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation and inference about preservation bias.

claim: Fossil adult female scale insects are very scarce probably because they are commonly sedentary or sessile on host plants.
source: However, their fossil record is over-dominated by males entrapped in fossil resins, and fossil adult females are very scarce—probably because they are commonly sedentary or sessile on host plants (Koteja, 2000).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation about scale insect behavior.

claim: The next oldest fossil adult female scale insect after Wathondara kotejai is from the late Eocene Baltic amber.
source: To our knowledge, the new fossil is the only Mesozoic record of an adult female, the next oldest being from the late Eocene Baltic amber (Koteja and Żak-Ogaza, 1988).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous fossil discovery.

claim: Wathondara kotejai is unambiguously referable to Ortheziidae based on its general habitus with body covered with wax plates, ensign-like ovisac, stalked eyes, and well-developed legs.
source: Wathondara kotejai is unambiguously referable to Ortheziidae, as evidenced by its general habitus with its body covered with wax plates, ensign-like ovisac, stalked eyes, and well-developed legs (Kozár, 2004).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations of the fossil and comparison with known Ortheziidae characteristics.

claim: Wathondara kotejai shares two potential synapomorphies with Recent and Tertiary, crown-group Ortheziidae: differentiated apical and subapical setae on the last antennal segment, and trochanter and femur fused.
source: Furthermore, W. kotejai shares two potential synapomorphies with Recent and Tertiary, crown-group Ortheziidae: differentiated apical and subapical setae on the last antennal segment, and trochanter and femur fused (Vea and Grimaldi, 2012).
evidence: This is based on morphological observations and comparison with known synapomorphies.

claim: Burmorthezia from mid-Cretaceous Burmese amber is considered an extinct sister group to the crown-group Ortheziidae.
source: Two Cretaceous genera have been tentatively attributed to Ortheziidae: Burmorthezia Vea and Grimaldi in mid-Cretaceous Burmese amber is considered as an extinct sister group to the crown-group Ortheziidae (Vea and Grimaldi, 2012), while Cretorthezia Koteja and Azar in Early Cretaceous Lebanese amber is probably a stem group of scale insects (Koteja and Azar, 2008; Hodgson and Hardy, 2013) or an extinct group within Ortheziidae (Vea and Grimaldi, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous taxonomic work.

claim: Cretorthezia from Early Cretaceous Lebanese amber is probably a stem group of scale insects or an extinct group within Ortheziidae.
source: Two Cretaceous genera have been tentatively attributed to Ortheziidae: Burmorthezia Vea and Grimaldi in mid-Cretaceous Burmese amber is considered as an extinct sister group to the crown-group Ortheziidae (Vea and Grimaldi, 2012), while Cretorthezia Koteja and Azar in Early Cretaceous Lebanese amber is probably a stem group of scale insects (Koteja and Azar, 2008; Hodgson and Hardy, 2013) or an extinct group within Ortheziidae (Vea and Grimaldi, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous taxonomic work showing uncertainty.

claim: The new fossil supports the view that crown-group Ortheziidae are present in the mid-Cretaceous.
source: Our new fossil supports the view that crown-group Ortheziidae are present in the mid-Cretaceous.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphological characteristics of the fossil.

claim: The seventh, eighth, ninth, and posterior wax lobes of W. kotejai are distinctly extended and cover the ovisac dorsally.
source: The seventh, eighth, ninth, and posterior wax lobes of W. kotejai are distinctly extended and cover the ovisac dorsally.
evidence: This is directly observed in the fossil specimen.

claim: The thick wax cover of W. kotejai not only protects the adult female but also serves to shelter her eggs and first instars.
source: The thick wax cover not only protects the adult female but also serves to shelter her eggs and first instars.
evidence: This is inferred from the morphology and comparison with extant species.

claim: Extant ortheziid females have a band of pores on the ventral side of the abdomen, which secrete a waxy ovisac.
source: Extant ortheziid females have a band of pores on the ventral side of the abdomen, which secrete a waxy ovisac.
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about extant species.

claim: The eggs and hatched nymphs are protected within the ovisac in extant ortheziids and monophlebids.
source: The eggs and hatched nymphs are protected within the ovisac (Figure 3), as in extant ortheziids and monophlebids (Vogelsang and Szklarzewicz, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation and comparison with the fossil.

claim: In extant species, young nymphs hatch within the ovisac and remain there for a few days until they have acquired a thin covering of wax secretion, then crawl out through a split in the wax at the distal end of the ovisac.
source: In extant species, the young nymphs hatch within this ovisac and remain there for a few days until they have acquired a thin covering of wax secretion (visible in our specimens as a slight white pubescence on the fossil nymphs), then crawl out through a split in the wax at the distal end of the ovisac (Gullan and Kosztarab, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and observation in the fossil.

claim: Extant first instars are mobile and serve as principle agents for dispersion and seeking out suitable feeding sites.
source: Extant first instars are mobile and serve as principle agents for dispersion and seeking out suitable feeding sites (Koteja, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Egg brooding is widely considered to be a primitive form of brood care.
source: This egg brooding is widely considered to be a primitive form of brood care (e.g., Royle, et al., 2012; Wong et al., 2013; Siveter et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Some Early Cretaceous cockroaches have been reported with an ootheca attached.
source: Some Early Cretaceous cockroaches have been reported with an ootheca attached (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005, Figure 7.72).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous fossil discovery.

claim: Cockroaches with attached oothecae are not definitive evidence of egg brooding because some cockroaches subsequently deposit the ootheca in a suitable crevice.
source: However, it is not definitive evidence of egg brooding, because some cockroaches subsequently deposit the ootheca in a suitable crevice.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of cockroach behavior.

claim: W. kotejai provides the earliest unequivocal evidence of brood care in insects.
source: Therefore, W. kotejai provides the earliest unequivocal evidence of brood care in insects.
evidence: This is inferred from the fossil evidence and comparison with other fossil records.

claim: Brood care is considered to have evolved independently in at least seven insect orders.
source: Brood care is considered to have evolved independently in at least seven insect orders (Wong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The most common forms of brood care are egg brooding and offspring attendance.
source: This remarkable behavior takes several forms of which the most common are egg brooding and offspring attendance.
evidence: This is stated as general knowledge about brood care.

claim: Some extant scale insect species possess an ovoviviparous form or pseudoplacental viviparity.
source: Some extant species (e.g., Diaspididae, some Pseudococcidae) even possess an ovoviviparous form or pseudoplacental viviparity (Gullan and Kosztarab, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Ovisacs occur in many scale insect families including Ortheziidae, Monophlebidae, unrelated Coccidae and many Pseudococcidae.
source: In addition to Ortheziidae, ovisacs occur in many other families, for example, Monophlebidae, unrelated Coccidae and many Pseudococcidae, in all of which the secretions of a variety of tubular ducts and disc-pores combine to form the ovisac (Ben-Dov et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a reference work.

claim: Various types of ovisacs have evolved convergently to protect offspring from wet and dry conditions, honeydew contamination, and natural enemies.
source: These various types of ovisacs have evolved convergently to protect their offspring from wet and dry conditions, honeydew contamination, and natural enemies (Gullan and Kosztarab, 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Behavioral and morphological adaptations associated with considerable maternal investment in scale insects were already well established by the mid-Cretaceous.
source: Our study demonstrates that these significant behavioral and morphological adaptations, associated with considerable maternal investment, were already well established by the mid-Cretaceous.
evidence: This is inferred from the fossil evidence.

claim: Many extant Ortheziidae females feed on roots and fungal mycelia or mosses and lichens.
source: Many extant Ortheziidae females feed on roots and fungal mycelia or mosses and lichens (Vea and Grimaldi, 2012) and 'run about' in forest litter with the eggs carried in the ovisac attached to their bodies.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Extant Ortheziidae females 'run about' in forest litter with the eggs carried in the ovisac attached to their bodies.
source: Many extant Ortheziidae females feed on roots and fungal mycelia or mosses and lichens (Vea and Grimaldi, 2012) and 'run about' in forest litter with the eggs carried in the ovisac attached to their bodies.
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about extant species behavior.

claim: The habit of carrying eggs in an ovisac is considered to be the most primitive habit in scale insects.
source: This is considered to be the most primitive habit in scale insects (Gullan and Kosztarab, 1997; Koteja, 2001), and similar brood care behavior also occurs in other early scale insects, for example, Margarodidae and Matsucoccidae (Koteja, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Similar brood care behavior occurs in other early scale insects, for example, Margarodidae and Matsucoccidae.
source: This is considered to be the most primitive habit in scale insects (Gullan and Kosztarab, 1997; Koteja, 2001), and similar brood care behavior also occurs in other early scale insects, for example, Margarodidae and Matsucoccidae (Koteja, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Brood care behavior in scale insects probably has an early origin and maybe a synapomorphy for scale insects.
source: Therefore, this behavior probably has an early origin and maybe a synapomorphy for scale insects.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of the behavior across basal scale insect families.

claim: Flowering plants and ants are thought to be important drivers for radiation of the neococcoids.
source: Flowering plants and ants are thought to be important drivers for radiation of the most diverse advanced group, the neococcoids (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Both flowering plants and ants are absent in the evolutionary history of basal groups of scale insects.
source: However, both factors are absent in the evolutionary history of basal groups of scale insects (Figure 4).
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic timing shown in Figure 4.

claim: Brood care could have been an important driver for the early radiation of scale insects which occurred during the end of the Jurassic or earliest Cretaceous.
source: Brood care, greatly promoting the survival of offspring (Royle et al., 2012), could therefore have been an important driver for the early radiation of scale insects which occurred during the end of the Jurassic or earliest Cretaceous (Figure 4).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the timing of radiation and the adaptive value of brood care.

claim: Direct evidence of brood care behavior has been reported only in Cenozoic ambers prior to this study.
source: Despite a great taxonomic diversity of extant insects with brood care (Wong et al., 2013), direct evidence of such behavior has been reported only in Cenozoic ambers (Peñalver et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous fossil discoveries.

claim: The new fossil is unique in providing evidence of ovarian and juvenile developmental stages in a fossil insect.
source: The new fossil is unique in providing evidence of ovarian and juvenile developmental stages in a fossil insect.
evidence: This is based on the presence of eggs and nymphs in the fossil.

claim: The new fossil highlights the long-term stasis of brood care behavior in archaeococcoids, extending nearly 100 million years.
source: More remarkably, it represents the earliest direct evidence of brood care in insects and highlights the long-term stasis of this behavior in archaeococcoids, extending nearly 100 million years.
evidence: This is inferred from the similarity between fossil and modern behavior over the time span.

claim: Burmese amber harbors the most diverse biota in amber from the Cretaceous.
source: Burmese amber (amber from northern Myanmar) harbors the most diverse biota in amber from the Cretaceous, and more than 200 families of arthropods have been reported from this deposit.
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about the Burmese amber deposit.

claim: More than 200 families of arthropods have been reported from Burmese amber.
source: Burmese amber (amber from northern Myanmar) harbors the most diverse biota in amber from the Cretaceous, and more than 200 families of arthropods have been reported from this deposit.
evidence: This is stated as knowledge about the Burmese amber deposit.

claim: The only commercial source of Burmese amber is the Hukawng Valley in Tanaing Township, Myitkyina District of Kachin State.
source: However, the only commercial source is the Hukawng Valley in Tanaing Township, Myitkyina District of Kachin State.
evidence: This is stated as factual information about the amber source.

claim: The amber under study is from an amber mine located near Noije Bum Village, Tanaing Town.
source: The amber under study is from an amber mine located near Noije Bum Village, Tanaing Town (Figure 1 in Kania et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated as factual information about the specimen locality.

claim: Four institutes have collected more than 100,000 amber pieces from the Noije Bum mine.
source: Four institutes (Nanjing Institute of Geology and Palaeontology, Lingpoge Amber Museum, Huxuan Amber Museum, and Fushun Amber Institute) have collected more than 100,000 amber pieces from this mine, and each piece commonly contains some insects.
evidence: This is stated as factual information about collection efforts.

claim: Burmese amber has been dated biostratigraphically from late Albian to Cenomanian (about 105 to 95 million years old), based on an ammonite and palynology.
source: Burmese amber has been dated biostratigraphically from late Albian to Cenomanian (about 105 to 95 million years old), based on an ammonite and palynology (Cruickshank and Ko, 2003; Ross et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous dating studies.

claim: U-Pb dating of zircons from the volcaniclastic matrix of Burmese amber gave an age of 98.8 ± 0.6 million years.
source: The U-Pb dating of zircons from the volcaniclastic matrix of the amber gave an age of 98.8 ± 0.6 million year (Shi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a radiometric dating study.

claim: The amber specimen preserves an adult female with about 60 elliptical eggs (0.3 mm long, 0.2 mm wide) in wax ovisac.
source: Amber specimen preserves adult female with about 60 elliptical eggs (0.3 mm long, 0.2 mm wide) in wax ovisac, and six first-instar nymphs near adult (Figure 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in the fossil specimen.

claim: The adult body of W. kotejai is elongate oval, 6 mm long, 2 mm wide (with ovisac).
source: Adult body elongate oval, 6 mm long, 2 mm wide (with ovisac).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the fossil specimen.

claim: The antenna of W. kotejai is about 1.2 mm long with eight segments.
source: Antenna about 1.2 mm long, inserted ventrally at frontal margin, with eight segments (Figure 2C)
evidence: This is a direct measurement and observation from the fossil specimen.

claim: The ovisac of W. kotejai is well-developed, 3 mm long, 2.1 mm wide.
source: Ovisac well-developed, 3 mm long, 2.1 mm wide (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement from the fossil specimen.

claim: Six associated first-instar nymphs are of similar size, 0.3 mm long, 0.2 mm wide, with only 6-segmented antennae.
source: Six associated first-instar nymphs are of similar size, 0.3 mm long, 0.2 mm wide, with only 6-segmented antennae (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is a direct measurement and observation from the fossil specimen.

claim: The holotype specimen BA14011 preserves an adult female with eggs, six first-instar nymphs, and a weevil.
source: BA14011. The amber piece preserves an adult female with eggs, six first-instar nymphs, and a weevil.
evidence: This is a direct observation of the holotype specimen contents.

claim: The holotype amber piece is polished in the form of a flattened ellipsoid cabochon, clear and transparent, with diameter about 11 mm, height about 5 mm, and weight about 0.8 g.
source: It is polished in the form of a flattened ellipsoid cabochon, clear and transparent, with diameter about 11 mm, height about 5 mm, and weight about 0.8 g.
evidence: This is a direct description and measurement of the physical specimen.

claim: Some evidence suggests that the amber was probably reworked before being deposited in the volcaniclastic matrix.
source: However, some evidence (e.g., high degree of roundness of amber, bivalve borings on the surface of the amber) suggests that the amber was probably reworked before being deposited in the volcaniclastic matrix.
evidence: This is inferred from taphonomic features of the amber.

claim: An early diversification of scale insects probably occurred during the end of the Jurassic or earliest Cretaceous.
source: An early diversification of scale insects probably occurred during the end of the Jurassic or earliest Cretaceous (blue area), and later radiations are probably closely related to the rise of angiosperms and ants (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation and shown in Figure 4.

claim: Later radiations of scale insects are probably closely related to the rise of angiosperms and ants.
source: An early diversification of scale insects probably occurred during the end of the Jurassic or earliest Cretaceous (blue area), and later radiations are probably closely related to the rise of angiosperms and ants (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Matsucoccidae, Ortheziidae, and Margarodidae are commonly considered as the most primitive families of scale insects.
source: Matsucoccidae, Ortheziidae, Margarodidae are commonly considered as the most primitive families (Vea and Grimaldi, 2015), but their phylogenetic relationships are still unresolved (e.g., Gullan and Cook, 2007; Hodgson and Hardy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies.

claim: The phylogenetic relationships among Matsucoccidae, Ortheziidae, and Margarodidae are still unresolved.
source: Matsucoccidae, Ortheziidae, Margarodidae are commonly considered as the most primitive families (Vea and Grimaldi, 2015), but their phylogenetic relationships are still unresolved (e.g., Gullan and Cook, 2007; Hodgson and Hardy, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous phylogenetic studies showing uncertainty.

claim: There are undescribed scale marks on plants from the Middle Triassic Dont Formation of Italy.
source: (1) Undescribed scale marks on plants from the Middle Triassic Dont Formation of Italy (T Wappler, personal observation, October 2014)
evidence: This is based on personal observation cited in the figure caption.

claim: There are scale marks on plants from the Late Triassic Molteno Formation of South Africa.
source: (2) scale marks on plants from the Late Triassic Molteno Formation of South Africa (Labandeira, 2006)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous trace fossil discovery.

claim: There is a putative, undescribed scale insect from the Late Jurassic.
source: (3) putative, undescribed scale insect from the Late Jurassic (Grimaldi and Engel, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.
